text: Eh, couldn't we have done without him now, but alas! Wasn't it, as it were, quite enough for only the official delegates to do the job, but Bay Ganyo had to stick his nose in as well? As if those, the official ones, were not capable of showing the outside world what a Bulgarian and Bulgarian patriotism mean. And weren't there enough characters like the man with the "full Russian beard," or that one who "looks like a little Frenchman and speaks French very briskly and fluently," or finally, the "famous Bulgarian diplomat"? Even if you ask me, the last one alone was enough for the Russians. The man whom the Russian press calls a "Bulgarian diplomat" is actually a soap-maker from Plovdiv. What a progressive nation! When Bulgarian soap-makers pass for diplomats in Russia, imagine what would happen if a real Bulgarian diplomat appeared before Mother Russia, eh? No matter how modest you are, you cannot help but feel proud! Indeed, justice requires one to admit that even the French resemble us a little: their Félix Faure went from being a tanner to the President of the Republic, and even the Romans have a similar case: do you remember Cincinnatus? But we shall surpass both. Try, for example, to stand in the middle of the marketplace blindfolded: I assure you that the first Bulgarian you catch and ask: "Do you wish to become a Bulgarian prince?" — without hesitating for a single minute, will answer you in the affirmative; perhaps he will only set the condition that the gifts and tips he hands out be paid not from his salary, but from the treasury...

The talk is about Bay Ganyo... So, that's the thing, couldn't we, I said, have done without him? Why did he too have to represent the Bulgarian people? But you will say that he is not an official delegate. No matter. Since correspondents from important newspapers go to interview him and his words, like an oracular prophecy, are spread through the press across the whole world — go then and prove that it is not the Bulgarian people speaking through Bay Ganyo's mouth...

But I, an incorrigible optimist, think that fate has intertwined Bai Ganyo into this mission solely so that the deputation might preserve its true Bulgarian national character, because, say what you will, a bushy Russian beard or a Frenchified diplomat—they do not sound Bulgarian. And that Bai Ganyo held high and with dignity the banner of Bulgarian patriotism, everyone will clearly see from the following interview. (There is no need to mention that the first gentleman dressed in a tailcoat who entered Bai Ganyo's room, and before whom Bai Ganyo managed to pour out his brotherly feelings, was not a correspondent, but a waiter from the hotel. A slight misunderstanding, but what can you do? Sincere feelings welling up in the chest, eyes clouded by touching tears—it is only too natural for a mistake to occur.)
A correspondent enters. Whether Bay Ganyo had prepared sliced onions for himself or not — I do not know, but I can positively assert that his eyes filled with tears:
— Oh, hello, brother, hello. Nine years, brother, nine! It’s not a day, it’s not two, nine years — and Bay Ganyo began to cry.

Everyone would think, quite naturally, that the brotherly meeting after a long, sad separation would overflow Bai Ganyo's breast with tender feelings, and the excess of these feelings would pour out in the form of touching tears; but what was the correspondent's astonishment when he saw that his interlocutor's face instantly cleared, and he heard from his mouth the following words, uttered as if stealthily, with a wink:

— But you should know what a wreath we’ve had made, it’s a beauty — a masterwork! Not just copper or silver — but pure gold. And do you know how much it costs? What do you think, brother?... If the Russians, for example, were to present me with such a wreath, so to speak, I would kiss their feet — what are you talking about, it’s no joke, gold! And pure gold at that, not just anything...
— Well, some kind of Macedonian movement has started over there in your parts — the correspondent diverts the conversation. — Do you find that this movement is timely?

— A movement? What movement?! — Bay Ganyo wonders, as if he is hearing about such a thing for the first time. — Don't you worry! There is no movement... Rascally business! Brigands! Is it even time for an uprising now? And what do those vagabonds want — I cannot understand. Your Honor, do you know what? I don't know if you know — there is a ferman from 1870 for six bishops in Macedonia — they have given three, they will give three more, and then they will all sit on their backsides! That is what they are after!
— Oh, shut those up... Let's talk about something else. Tell me, do you know Dragan Tsankov?
— Yes, I think I know him quite well.
— Well? — and Bay Ganyo reinforced the question with an ambiguous movement of his fingers. — How does this fellow seem to you?
— I think he is a good patriot.

Bay Ganyo laughed unnaturally and shook his head:
— A pa-tri-ot, is he? E-he-e, if you only knew what kind of goods he is! Has he thought for even one day about his fatherland? He only looks to settle himself and his son-in-law. He’s been like that since he was little, don’t I know him. If you’re asking for patriots, we are the real patriots. Look at me well! Don’t give me two hundred — just fix me a hundred and fifty rubles a month, and you’ll see what your Uncle Ganyo can do... How do you reckon me, your honor! This isn’t Abyssinia...
— Have you had lunch, Mr. Balkanski?
— Why do you ask? Are you going to invite me to lunch, or what?... I accept. Aren't we Slavs?
